name: Priya Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team maintaining ticketing software for a tech company, and I have a master’s degree. I check how the system gives each buyer a seat, especially before a large Friday sale. I like making a crowded event work for ordinary buyers, but I hate the call when two people turn up holding the same number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the ticketing team that small AI helpers may speed up routine error reports, but a sold seat must still belong to one person. I do not use AI tools; I want to know who changed the code before a big sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn well for a lead developer and have about ten months of basic expenses saved. There are plenty of software firms nearby, so a modest change would not make me fear for next month’s pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing the seat-allocation code with my team and ask our customer desk for the complaints after each sale. In the first year I’d leave my savings untouched and keep putting 300 a month aside if pay holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about my own job. The Friday evening sale can still be stressful, but a small tool does not change who answers the buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which complaint do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A buyer reached the venue with two people holding the same seat number. I stayed on the phone until the desk found a second seat, and the software fault was ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not try even a small AI helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have seen coworkers paste a private customer log into a tool without checking where it goes. I would rather review the report myself until our rules are clear.

say: I think **ticket errors** still need an engineer who can explain a sold seat.
I want a **named reviewer** before code changes ahead of a major sale.
think: I have **ten months saved** and high lead-developer pay.
I see **plenty of local firms** if this small change ever unsettles my team.
do: **Keep reviewing** seat-allocation code and ask the customer desk for sale complaints.
**Save 300 monthly** if my current pay holds.
feel: **Calm** about income, though major sales remain stressful.
S0.quote: A buyer reached the venue with two people holding the same seat number.
fieldNote: She treats the **double-sold seat** as an accountable service failure.
High pay, **ten months saved** and local openings support a calm baseline despite sale-night pressure.

steps.text: Keep reviewing ticket seat-allocation code with the current team
Save 300 monthly while lead-developer pay holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our staff council that management needs to show which coding and customer tasks move to AI. I would ask for paid training and a rule against feeding customer details into outside tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think routine bug reports and test code could go quickly, leaving fewer developers to manage sale nights. My own hours or bonus could shrink, even with ten months saved, and I have never practised with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the staff council meeting this month and ask it to seek written staffing and data rules. In the first year of strong change I’d take a paid workplace AI lesson on our safe test server if offered; I would not upload real buyer records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my role and the people who answer calls. Money buys time, but it does not teach me the tool overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a tool after refusing it for so long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would on paid time with fake tickets and a colleague checking the output. I want to see it find a double sale before I use it on anything important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the council to win first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written count of roles and a clear rule for customer data. Without those, an AI rollout could turn a careful team into a smaller one carrying the same blame.

say: I want the **staff council** to see which coding and customer tasks move to AI.
I want **paid training** and a rule protecting buyer records.
think: I expect **routine test work** to shrink and sale-night responsibility to remain.
I fear my **hours or bonus** could shrink despite a strong cash cushion.
do: **Join the staff council** meeting and request written staffing and data rules.
**Learn workplace AI** on fake tickets only if a paid lesson is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about my hours, bonus and customer desk colleagues.
S1.quote: Money buys time, but it does not teach me the tool overnight.
fieldNote: Her **never-used-AI habit** makes paid supervised practice a meaningful change.
The **data rule** matters to her as much as headcount because real buyer records are sensitive.

steps.text: Join staff council talks on staffing and buyer-data rules
Attend a paid AI lesson using fake tickets if the company offers one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 can do almost all the design and coding I lead, so the company must tell workers what happens to their jobs. Robots around 2031 may matter to venue staff, but they do not delay the change to my screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead role could end even though I am good at it, and other nearby tech firms might be cutting too. Ten months of savings helps me breathe but will not buy a permanent career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the staff council now to seek a written notice period and paid retraining terms. I’d also stop looking for a larger flat; if the role ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid ticketing support roles only where there are openings and keep my savings for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed by the speed. I could pay bills for a while, but I would not know which job still needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your partner about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Leila that we should keep our current lease while my job is exposed. She works too, but a bigger rent would tie both of us to a bet we do not need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for retraining yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy an expensive course just because the sales pitch promises safety. I would join a paid course if a real employer funded it and named the work it prepares me for.

say: I want **job plans** published before full AGI reaches our code in 2028.
I see **venue robots** around 2031 as later than my screen-work risk.
think: I expect my **lead role** could end despite strong skills.
I know **ten months saved** cannot buy a permanent career if firms cut together.
do: **Seek paid training** and notice terms through the staff council now.
**Keep the current flat** instead of committing to higher rent with Leila.
**Apply for paid support** in ticketing after a cut only where openings exist.
feel: **Alarmed** by fast job loss, despite savings for bills.
S2.quote: Ten months of savings helps me breathe but will not buy a permanent career.
fieldNote: Her **cash cushion** softens immediate bills but not a sector-wide loss of developer roles.
She keeps **rent flexibility** and rejects an unfunded course with no named job.

steps.text: Ask the staff council to seek written notice and paid retraining terms
Keep the current flat instead of signing a larger lease with Leila
Apply for paid ticketing support where openings exist after a layoff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues that five years gives us time to set fair rules for AI-made ticket changes. I would ask the staff council to check whether the company offers paid routes into customer dispute work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI in 2031 still reaches most of my day, and robots around 2034 do not give my coding work extra time. I might use five years to build a larger cushion and learn the dispute side before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for one paid shift per month with ticket complaints, and take it only if the support director agrees. I’d save 250 a month while my pay holds; if a paid dispute vacancy remains after 2031, I’d apply before leaving my developer job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, but less trapped than with two years. The shift must be on company time; I will not volunteer my way into a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on that shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d listen to buyers explain why a refund did not fix a ruined evening. I know the code path, but I have not sat through enough of those calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the director says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my current duties and ask the council to raise paid transfers in its next meeting. I would not list an unapproved shift as experience.

say: I want **fair rules** for AI-made ticket changes before 2031.
I want the **staff council** to check paid routes into customer disputes.
think: I still face **thinking AI in 2031** ahead of robots around 2034.
I could build a **larger cushion** and learn complaint work if shifts are funded.
do: **Request paid complaint shifts** monthly and take them only with director approval.
**Save 250 monthly** while pay holds; apply for paid dispute vacancies if available after 2031.
feel: **Anxious but less trapped** with time to test an approved paid route.
S3.quote: I will not volunteer my way into a new career.
fieldNote: Her **shift request** tests actual complaint work without risking unpaid time.
She makes the **2031 move** conditional on a paid vacancy, not a training promise.

steps.text: Take monthly paid ticket complaint shifts only if the support director approves
Save 250 monthly while developer pay holds
Apply for paid dispute vacancies if available after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade lets workers insist on rules before full AGI reaches ticketing code in 2036. I would rather learn from real buyers than pretend every new software tool is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I could have a larger buffer and know whether dispute work suits me. Robots for venue tasks would follow around 2039, but my developer role would face thinking AI three years earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading code reviews this year and ask for funded shadowing with customer support twice a year. I’d take those visits only if approved, and separately save toward a year of basic expenses while wages hold. If my developer role ends after 2036, I’d seek paid dispute work only if posts exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy, not relaxed. More time helps me test a second skill, but I still need a company willing to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you accept a dispute role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want the pay in writing and a clear manager to call when a customer needs a decision. If it pays much less than my current job, I would ask what bills Leila and I can safely cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about AI policy at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the staff council to demand an audit of customer data leaving our systems. A buyer should not have to guess where a complaint transcript went.

say: I want **worker rules** settled before full AGI reaches ticketing code in 2036.
I would learn from **real buyers** before trusting new tools.
think: I could build a **larger buffer** and test complaint work by 2036.
I expect **developer work** to change before venue robots arrive around 2039.
do: **Keep leading code reviews** while requesting funded customer-support shadowing twice yearly.
**Attend shadowing visits** only if funded and approved; separately save toward a year of expenses while wages hold.
**Seek paid dispute work** only if my developer role ends after 2036 and posts exist.
feel: **Uneasy**, though the longer runway allows a paid skills test.
S4.quote: A buyer should not have to guess where a complaint transcript went.
fieldNote: Her long plan preserves **code review wages** while seeking funded customer contact.
Her **data concern** remains active even with time and savings; she wants the council to audit complaint records leaving company systems.

steps.text: Keep leading ticketing code reviews while employed
Shadow customer support twice yearly only if funded and approved
Save toward a year of expenses while wages hold
Seek paid dispute work only if displaced after 2036 and posts exist

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking work I lead could end across many firms at once. Written notice, company-paid training and an actual paid opening in customer disputes would help more than an expensive course advertisement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a buyer learns where their complaint went after a software error. I want a named person and a rule about customer records leaving our system.

headlineQuote: I would not buy an expensive course just because the sales pitch promises safety.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old ticketing lead** with a master’s degree, high pay and roughly ten months of expenses saved.
She **never uses AI** and demands named reviewers and clear rules for buyer data.
Her strong savings and **many local firms** keep AI Plateau calm, while job cuts under Steady Disruption threaten hours or bonus.
The **2028 shock** alarms her because coding could vanish before a funded dispute role exists.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead role across firms despite ten months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, company-paid training and a real paid dispute vacancy would support a move.
